4. Detailed Rationale.

The University of Guam is the only identified resource capable of meeting these urgent needs. Their Department of Agriculture/Biosecurity Division has trained personnel and canine teams experienced in detecting the species of concern, and their proximity allows for immediate deployment. Prompt canine inspections are essential to prevent the spread of the Little Fire Ants and Coconut Rhinoceros Beetle in CNMI. Delays would significantly harm government interests by increasing ecological and economic risks, complicating FEMA recovery, and raising long-term eradication costs. For example, the Coconut Rhinoceros Beetle population has decimated 90% of Guam’s endemic cycads which was listed as the most abundant tree in Guam’s forests in a 2002 forestry survey. As a result, this plant was added to the National Endangered Species List in 2015. The second most abundant tree on Guam was the coconut palm, but it they have also been severely damaged and killed by this beetle.
